verdicts.rewritten_summary: BuzzFeed News feature (12 Jan 2018): in France, where prisoners are placed by the sex on their ID under Article D248 of the criminal procedure code, transgender women held in male prisons fall into a legal grey area and are 'punished for a lot more than their alleged crimes' — the piece follows cases including a trans woman held at Lille in 2014 amid inmate threats. French framework applying to Réunion as a department.

Opinion of 25 May 2021 of the French places-of-deprivation-of-liberty watchdog (CGLPL): finds 'the persistence of serious violations' of transgender detainees' fundamental rights across French custody facilities, based on referrals since 2010 covering some forty transgender persons, interviews with associations and experts, and on-site/document inspections, with recommendations to the Interior, Justice and Health ministries. National framework covering Réunion.

PinkNews (26 Aug 2012): PM Jean-Marc Ayrault announced the same-sex marriage and adoption bill would go to the National Assembly and Senate in October 2012, fulfilling President Hollande's campaign pledge; both houses had to approve, and the Catholic Bishops Conference came out against adoption. The marriage statute that subsequently applied to Réunion with the 2013 metropolitan law.

Yagg (25 Jul 2012, French): the harassment bill adopted by the National Assembly amended Penal Code article L225-1 to add 'identité sexuelle' as a discrimination ground, making transphobia prosecutable; deputies Sergio Coronado (EELV) and Elisabeth Pochon (PS) intervened in the debate. This is the discrimination-protection basis in force in Réunion.

Yagg (19 May 2016, French): the National Assembly adopted amendment 282 — tabled by about forty Socialist deputies — inserting a Civil Code section to facilitate legal gender change for trans people, though the government's three sub-amendments could limit its scope. The gender-change framework applying to Réunion as state law.

ACCEPT Romania (31 Mar 2026): the Sector 6 Court of Bucharest ordered a new birth certificate for trans man Arian Mirzarafie-Ahi reflecting his UK-recognised identity, and the ruling became definitive after the Bucharest Tribunal rejected appeals filed by the Cluj civil-status directorates — building on the CJEU's 2024 ruling that member states must transcribe intra-EU legal gender recognition. Announced on Trans Day of Visibility; ACCEPT urges others who changed documents in another EU country to pursue transcription in Romania.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2026 (covering Jan–Dec 2025): anti-LGBTI rhetoric intensified during the 2025 presidential campaign — candidate Călin Georgescu declared himself 'against LGBTQ' in February and PM Ciolacu mocked gender-marker changes; the National Audiovisual Council issued a public warning to B1 TV in August over anti-Pride 'provocation' framing after an ACCEPT complaint; a Ploiești deputy mayor of AUR made further derogatory announcements.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2024 (covering 2023): the CNCD investigated printing houses that refused to print LGBT and gender-equality materials; the IPSOS PRIDE 2023 survey found 51% of Romanians agree same-sex families should enjoy legal recognition; March 2024 education-law drafts carried anti-discrimination provisions that drew 13 religious groups' protests and a 50+ organisation counter-response.

Outright International Romania overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): same-sex relations legal nationwide; GO 137/2000 covers sex and sexual orientation but institutional follow-through is limited; no marriage or civil unions (the 2018 constitution-ban referendum failed on low turnout; the Orthodox Church has opposed a civil-partnership bill since 2017); legal gender recognition possible; LGBTI organisations can register.

ILGA-Europe and partners' submission to the EU 2025 Rule of Law Report (2025), with ACCEPT Romania authoring the Romania chapter (p.29): of nine country submissions, eight reported smear campaigns, disinformation and hate speech against LGBTI people — the surge in anti-LGBTI narratives during the Romanian election period is cited as the clearest example of rights-impacting rule-of-law erosion.

FRA-commissioned legal study (Feb 2008) by Romanița Elena Iordache and Iustina Ionescu: maps how Romanian law implemented the EU Employment Directive 2000/78/EC and free-movement rules for LGBT partners — national anti-discrimination concepts, CNCD enforcement powers and NGO complaints; a dated baseline for Romania's protection architecture.

UK Home Office country policy note on sexual orientation/gender identity and expression (v2.0, June 2025; page updated 12 Aug 2026): affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia — including the autonomous republic of Chechnya — constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, setting the assessment standard for UK asylum claims. External-protection framework, dated 2025-26.

Human Rights Watch (30 Jun 2025): Russian courts have issued 101 'extremism'-related convictions for alleged participation in the 'International LGBT Movement' or displaying its alleged symbols; the charges span administrative and criminal codes, and HRW calls on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia.

Meduza (19 Jun 2025): after the Supreme Court's 2023 designation of the non-existent 'international LGBT movement' as extremist, cases under Russia's propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, and fines under those statutes brought over 60 million rubles ($765,300) into the state budget in the past two years alone.

The Moscow Times (23 Jun 2025): arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life in Russia through 2025 — a St Petersburg queer woman describes waking up to find herself 'a second-class citizen' after the Supreme Court's extremist designation.

BBC Russian (27 Jul 2024): follows 'Ada', a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a Siberian conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk — held for nine months, forced to take testosterone, pray and do manual labour before escaping when police responded to a phone she found — a documented account of coercive conversion practice against trans people in Russia.

Novaya Gazeta Europe (29 Jun 2024): after Putin signed the law prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents, for many transgender Russians emigration has become the only means of survival; profiles those caught in limbo between leaving and staying.

The Guardian (17 Jan 2024): within 48 hours of the Supreme Court's extremist designation, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars — about 100 patrons at one venue ordered to face walls, searched and photographed — with at least two other venues raided the same night, showing the speed of the post-ruling crackdown.

Outright International Rwanda overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): same-sex intimacy is not criminalised, but the Human Rights First Rwanda Association's 2025 submission to the UN Human Rights Committee documents law-enforcement abuses against transgender people — harassment at identity checks and arbitrary arrests on 'vagrancy'/'public order' grounds; LGBTIQ organisations cannot register openly, a public Pride event was held in 2021, and NGO Law No. 058/2024 (adopted June 2024) raises freedom-of-association concerns.

Vice (20 Nov 2020): reports violent detentions of transgender people in Rwanda: On Christmas day in 2018, Bella was walking out of a hotel in Kigali, Rwanda’s capital city, where she had been booked to sing for the holiday. After her show, she celebrated with friends and enjoyed the afternoon at the hotel bar. Stepping onto the street to make her way home, Bella— whose name has been changed due to concerns for her safety—was stopped by police officers. “I had my service card that showed I was working ther

KT Press (25 Sep 2016): asked at Rwanda Cultural Day in San Francisco about LGBT life in Rwanda, President Kagame replied 'it hasn't been our problem. And we don't intend to make it our problem'; the piece cites Article 26 of the constitution, which recognises only civil monogamous marriage between a man and a woman.

Queerstory Files blog (8 Oct 2012): historical overview of the Great Lakes region — anthropologists report that same-sex relations among young Tutsi and Hutu men existed pre-colonisation but were private and secret; situates Rwanda alongside Uganda and Burundi (independence 1962) and post-1994 genocide memory. Background/history, not current visitor risk.

LegalClarity (4 Jun 2026): Saudi Arabia criminalises same-sex conduct and gender nonconformity with no codified penal code — judges apply an uncodified sharia interpretation; penalties range from flogging and lengthy imprisonment to death in the most severe cases; visitor-facing explainer of the laws, how enforcement works and rules for visitors.

Outright International Saudi Arabia overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): criminal penalties are based on Shari'a; same-sex relations illegal for men and women; no legal gender recognition; LGBTI organisations cannot register anywhere in the country.

Cairo 52 Legal Research Institute Saudi Arabia profile (MENA Trans Archives): deviating from traditional gender norms is itself treated as a criminal offence; regional legal-research framing of gender-nonconformity provisions and their enforcement.

Wikipedia 'LGBTQ rights in Saudi Arabia' (fetched 2026): same-sex conduct illegal with penalties including capital punishment, indeterminate prison terms, flogging and fines; no gender-identity recognition, no discrimination protections, no same-sex relationship recognition; law uncodified on a Wahhabist interpretation of sharia (Quran/Sunnah), with enforcement-case and living-conditions sections. Reference overview.

BBC News: 'Meeno' — Mohammad Amin, a Pakistani transgender woman — died in Saudi custody after a roundup with 34 others in Azizia prison, Riyadh; Pakistani activists say she was beaten with clubs and hosepipes aggravating a chronic heart condition, while Saudi authorities attributed the death to a heart attack; family and trans-rights activists dispute the official account. Directly relevant to how Saudi enforcement treats trans people.

Gulf News (25 Oct 2021): five Saudi men were arrested in the Northern Borders province after filming themselves in women's clothing and posting the footage on social media — cross-dressing/gender-nonconformity enforced as a criminal matter.

Amnesty International (29 Jun 2026, updated 17 Jul 2026): documents visitors imprisoned over social media posts — including a business analyst arrested at Riyadh airport on 31 Aug 2024 as he was returning to the UK with his family, targeted for posts published before he even arrived in the country. Enforcement reaches travellers for expression, not only conduct on the ground.

UK FCDO Saudi Arabia safety advice (current): same-sex relations are illegal although legal action is uncommon; couples should avoid public affection; VisitSaudi states all visitors are welcome and privacy will be respected; being transgender is not recognised — trans travellers could face difficulties with dress codes and access to medical care.

A3M Global Monitoring LGBTQ+ Risk Map (2024/25): Saudi Arabia appears among the least safe destinations for LGBTQ travellers in a ranking that also lists Somalia, Yemen, Uganda, Afghanistan, UAE, Tanzania, Malaysia and Pakistan; page also profiles safest destinations (Iceland: self-ID, marriage since 2010).

Cairo 52 Sudan profile: penal code Article 152 criminalises wearing clothing of the opposite sex (cross-dressing provisions); no arrest statistics for trans people but documented state violence including extrajudicial killings against LGBTQIA+ individuals; no legal gender recognition, gender-affirming healthcare legally constrained, the ongoing conflict further restricts access, and state reliance on Sunni fatwas blocks transition. Gender-nonconformity framing for visitor risk.

Rainbow Sudan — Sudan's community magazine: runs sections on LGBTI rights in Sudan (history and analysis), a profile of Sudan and LGBTI organisations, i.e. documents an organised local community presence. Landing/index page: thin for current findings.

76crimes (15 Jul 2020): Sudan's Sovereign Council removed the death penalty for homosexuality — maximum now life imprisonment for a third offence — abolished the 100 lashes for same-sex intimacy, and set up to five years' imprisonment for a first offence in the criminal-code amendment.

76crimes (16 Jul 2024): anti-LGBT forces in Senegal are pushing for 15-year prison sentences for gay sex, up from the current maximum of five years — a debate running since 2020, with abuses against LGBT+ people commonplace in the West African nation.

BBC News: two men were jailed in Senegal for criticising opposition leader Ousmane Sonko — months and fined 100,000 CFA francs ($165, £130) each. They had been angered that Mr Sonko had allowed a visiting French politician to express his support for same-sex marriages. Homosexual acts are banned in the mainly Muslim West African country and are punishable by up to five years in prison. The political activist and the preacher were arrested two weeks ago after posting a video attacking Mr Sonko for giving a platform t

76crimes (24 Sep 2018): four LGBT people — two women and two men — were detained in Dakar for 'acts against the order of nature' amid a wave of politically motivated arrests ahead of the 2019 elections, triggered after videos circulated.

Metro (Nov 2023): a man's body was dug up and burned in the street in Senegal after it was revealed he was gay — exhumed and set on fire in the street after locals are said to have found out he was gay, in a case that has shocked the West African country. Four men have been arrested in connection with the incident, though images from the scene show a crowd of hundreds gathering around the fire. The 31-year-old man, named locally as Cheikh Fall, had been buried in Léona Niassene cemetery i

MPSC report (Feb 2025): transgender community faces several key challenges to health and well-being. These include (1) the difficult process of legal gender recognition, which has a prohibitive cost due to the required genital surgeries; (2) discrimination, abuse and restrictions facing transgender students; (3) discrimination against transgender persons in the employment sector; (4) discrimination and harassment in healthcare settings that discourag

Outright International Singapore overview (updated March 2026): same-sex relations legal for men and women; legal gender recognition possible; LGBTI organisations cannot register — registration remains the structural gap despite decriminalisation.

Straits Times (15 Nov 2023): the Singapore Prison Service reported 10 transgender inmates currently behind bars and no recorded cases of assault against transgender inmates — a rare official datum on trans prisoners in the system.

Pink Dot SG (8 Jan 2025): the new Workplace Fairness Legislation gives Singapore its first statutory anti-discrimination framework, but it stops short of covering LGBTQ+ workers — gender identity/expression are not protected grounds, leaving workplace exposure for trans staff.

South China Morning Post (3 Jul 2025): a clause of the radio broadcast code grouping homosexuality with paedophilia and incest as forbidden 'lifestyles' sparked calls for review — a former radio DJ and actor argued the grouping 'has no place in a post-377A Singapore'. Media-regulation residue after decriminalisation.

F&M Global Barometers Singapore country profile: interactive scores across unified/gay/transgender rights indices and an LGBTQI+ perception index, 2011–2024, covering de jure protections and lived experience — score values are served dynamically and are not extractable from the fetched text.

Intrepid Travel 'Is Singapore LGBTQIA+ friendly': describes a thriving LGBTQIA+ social scene — gay-friendly bars (e.g. Backstage Bar in Chinatown), pop-ups and exhibitions — alongside practical guidance on solo travel and room sharing for its own trips. Visitor-facing operator guidance.
